facts.text: > Strategy before copy. Every word of marketing copy rests on a value proposition - if the offer is weak, no headline can save it.
This skill lives at the strategy layer: designing the offer and the value proposition that copywriters then express. It spans three integrated disciplines:
Value-proposition design - mapping what customers need (jobs/pains/gains) to what you provide (pain relievers/gain creators) until fit is achieved.
Positioning - deciding which competitive frame to fight in and where you win.
Offer construction - stacking the deliverables, bonuses, and guarantees into an irresistible bundle.
The canvas maps two sides against each other until they achieve fit.
#### Customer Profile (right side - what they need)
Prioritization rule: Not all jobs/pains/gains are equal. Rank them by importance to the customer (extreme → moderate → minor) and focus pain relievers/gain creators on the top-ranked.
#### Value Map (left side - what you offer)

Fit is achieved when your pain relievers and gain creators explicitly address the customer's most important pains and gains. A strong fit typically covers the top 3–5 pains/gains that matter most. Fit is not permanent - market conditions and customer expectations shift it over time.

Jobs-to-Be-Done lens: Clayton Christensen's JTBD framing adds depth here: customers "hire" products to do a job. Ask "what job is the customer firing their current solution from?" to find the switching trigger.
Interview or observe customers; fill the profile side first (never project).
Map your existing offering against the populated profile.
Identify gaps: which high-priority pains/gains have no corresponding reliever/creator?
Redesign the offering or reframe it to close the highest-value gaps.
Test fit hypotheses in the market; iterate.

Dunford's insight: positioning is not a tagline exercise - it's a strategic decision about which competitive frame you let prospects use to evaluate you. Wrong frame = loss before the conversation starts.
#### The Five Positioning Components
Process: Start bottom-up with your best current customers. Ask why they love you; that reveals what unique attributes they actually value. Work backward from there to frame the category.
Category choice decision:
Use this as an internal alignment tool, not customer-facing copy. Write multiple variants per segment, then test message-market fit.

Message-market fit: A value proposition has message-market fit when the language you use mirrors the language customers use to describe their own problem - not the language you use to describe your solution.

Category design is the most aggressive positioning move: instead of competing in an existing category, you define a new one and condition the market to need it. Ramadan et al. report that category kings typically capture ~76% of the total economic value in their category (Play Bigger, 2016) - a practitioner claim based on their own market analysis, not an independently replicated figure.
Use category design when:
Your unique attributes are so differentiated that no existing category frames them fairly.
You can invest in educating the market (content, POV, thought leadership) over 3–5 years.
Your runway supports being early to a category before it tips.
Caution: Category creation is expensive. Most SMBs and early-stage products should compete in existing categories with differentiated positioning (Dunford) before attempting category creation.
Hormozi's central formula:
To maximize value:
Raise Dream Outcome - make the end state vivid and emotionally resonant.
Raise Perceived Likelihood - proof, testimonials, credentials, track record.
Lower Time Delay - speed of first result matters more than total time to full outcome.
Lower Effort & Sacrifice - remove friction, provide done-for-you components.
Practitioner note: This formula is heuristic, not derived from controlled research. Treat it as a diagnostic checklist, not a literal equation.
The offer stack bundles the core deliverable with supporting elements so total perceived value far exceeds the price. Hormozi's five-step process:
Identify the dream outcome in the customer's language.
List every obstacle between the customer and that outcome.
Create a solution for each obstacle (these become stack components).
Trim high-cost, low-value components; keep high-value, low-cost ones.
Name and price the stack so each component has a stated individual value; total stated value should substantially exceed the asking price.
Stack component types:
Guarantees shift risk from buyer to seller. Types by strength:

Design principle: The stronger the guarantee, the higher the perceived likelihood in the value equation - which raises value without changing price. Strong guarantees also self-select serious buyers (fewer refund requests than expected when the product delivers).

Rule: If the scarcity condition is not real, do not state or imply it. Manufactured urgency is deceptive, erodes trust on repeat exposure, and in several jurisdictions violates FTC guidance on "drip pricing" and false urgency. Cross-reference deceptive-design-and-dark-patterns for legal exposure details.
Price anchoring in offer design (distinct from pricing analytics):

Stack anchoring: State each component's individual value before presenting the bundled price. Thaler's transaction utility theory explains why bundled perceived value exceeds the sum of parts when presented correctly.
Decoy anchoring: Ariely's subscription study shows a mid-tier decoy makes the premium tier appear high-value; use this in tiered offer design.
Framing: Monthly vs. annual presentation affects affordability perception even when total cost is identical. Choose the frame that reduces perceived effort/sacrifice.
Label as behavioral framing, not manipulation: These are presentation choices. The underlying offer must deliver genuine value or the anchoring backfires on retention and refunds.

facets.title: Part 4 — Objection Handling in Offer Design

facts.text: Objections are unresolved pains or unanswered gains from the Value Proposition Canvas. A well-designed offer pre-empts them structurally:
Osterwalder, A., Pigneur, Y., Bernarda, G., & Smith, A. (2014). Value Proposition Design. Wiley. - Canonical source for VPC, jobs/pains/gains, fit.
Dunford, A. (2019). Obviously Awesome: How to Nail Product Positioning so Customers Get It, Buy It, Love It. Self-published. - Five-component positioning framework.
Moore, G. A. (1991, revised 2014). Crossing the Chasm. HarperBusiness. - Positioning statement template; technology adoption lifecycle.

Hormozi, A. (2021). $100M Offers: How to Make Offers So Good People Feel Stupid Saying No. Acquisition.com Press. - Value equation, offer stack, guarantee types. [Practitioner lore - not peer-reviewed research.]
Ramadan, A., Peterson, D., Lochhead, C., & Maney, K. (2016). Play Bigger: How Pirates, Dreamers, and Innovators Create and Dominate Markets. HarperBusiness. - Category design discipline.
Ariely, D., & Prelec, D. (2003). "Coherent Arbitrariness: Stable Demand Curves Without Stable Preferences." Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(1), 73–105. - Price anchoring research.
Thaler, R. H. (1985). "Mental Accounting and Consumer Choice." Marketing Science, 4(3), 199–214. - Transaction utility; bundle pricing psychology.
Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). "Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases." Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131. - Anchoring as cognitive heuristic.
Cialdini, R. B. (2001). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion. HarperCollins. - Scarcity as social-proof mechanism.

Eisend, M. (2022). "Scarcity Tactics in Marketing: A Meta-Analysis of Product Scarcity Effects on Consumer Purchase Intentions." Journal of Retailing, 98(4), 698–719. - Empirical support for scarcity effectiveness and ethical limits.

Christensen, C. M., Hall, T., Dillon, K., & Duncan, D. S. (2016). Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice. HarperBusiness. - Jobs-to-be-Done framework as complement to VPC.
Worchel, S., Lee, J., & Adewole, A. (1975). "Effects of Supply and Demand on Ratings of Object Value." Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(5), 906–914. - Classic scarcity experiment.

Anderson, J. C., Narus, J. A., & van Rossum, W. (2006). "Customer Value Propositions in Business Markets." Harvard Business Review, 84(3), 90–99. - Distinguishes all-benefits, favorable points of difference, and resonating-focus VP types; research-grounded counterpart to Osterwalder.
Lanning, M. J., & Michaels, E. G. (1988). "A Business is a Value Delivery System." McKinsey Staff Paper No. 41. - Original "value delivery system" framing; precursor to the value-proposition canon.

Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1979). "Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk." Econometrica, 47(2), 263–292. - Loss aversion and framing effects; theoretical grounding for why guarantees and loss-frame offers outperform gain-frame equivalents.

A new product launch where the marketing team wants to write copy before anyone has validated that the offer itself solves a real, prioritized customer pain — the Value Proposition Canvas forces the customer-need side to be filled in first.
